at hade.explanation: "At hade" means to hate, and it is a strong word. Danes often use something milder like "Jeg kan ikke lide" (I don't like) for everyday things. You can still say "Jeg hader at vente" (I hate waiting) when you really mean it. The opposite is "at elske". The word for hate is "et had".

sentence.en: I hate getting up early.

at handle.explanation: "At handle" means to shop, and also to act. "Jeg handler i supermarkedet" means "I shop at the supermarket". You can say "at handle ind" for doing the grocery shopping. A shopping trip is "en indkøbstur". With a different meaning, "handle om" means to be about: "Filmen handler om kærlighed".

sentence.en: I do my shopping at the supermarket.

at have.explanation: "At have" means to have or to own, and Danes also use it to build the "have done" form of most other words: "Jeg har spist" (I have eaten). The form "har" is the same for every person. A tip: Danish says "Jeg har fødselsdag" (I have birthday) where English says "It's my birthday".

sentence.da: Jeg **har** en bror og to søstre.
sentence.en: I have a brother and two sisters.

at have brug for.explanation: Means "to need" and is followed by whatever you need: "jeg har brug for hjælp" (I need help). Literally it is "have use for". Another way to say need is "at behøve", but "have brug for" is the everyday choice for needing things.

sentence.en: I need help.

at have fødselsdag.explanation: "At have fødselsdag" means to have a birthday, as in the day is your birthday. Danes say "Jeg har fødselsdag i dag" (It's my birthday today). To congratulate someone, you say "Tillykke med fødselsdagen!". Danes also often put out flags on birthdays.

sentence.en: My brother has a birthday tomorrow.

forms.en: I have had a pain in

at have ondt i.explanation: Use this to say that a body part hurts. Put the body part after it: "jeg har ondt i hovedet" (I have a headache) or "ondt i maven" (a stomach ache). The body part has "the" on the end, like "hovedet" or "maven". Literally it means "have pain in".

sentence.en: I have a headache.

at have på.explanation: "At have på" means to wear, or to have something on. Literally it is "to have on". You say "Hvad har du på?" (What are you wearing?). To put something on is "at tage på", and to take it off is "at tage af". Do not use "at bære" for clothes in everyday talk, since it mostly means to carry.

sentence.en: She is wearing a red jacket.

at have ret.explanation: Danish says "have right" where English says "be right", so use "have", not "er". "Du har ret" means "you are right". The opposite is "at have uret" (to be wrong). Do not say "jeg er rigtig" for this, which sounds odd.

sentence.da: Du **har ret**, det er for dyrt.
sentence.en: You are right, it's too expensive.

at have travlt.explanation: "At have travlt" means to be busy or in a hurry. Danish says "have" (to have) where English says "be": "Jeg har travlt" is literally "I have busy". It covers both being busy with work and being in a rush. The opposite is "at have tid" (to have time).

sentence.en: I am busy today.

at hedde.explanation: "At hedde" means to be called, and it is how you give your name: "Jeg hedder Anna" means 'My name is Anna'. It is also used for things, for example "Hvad hedder det på dansk?" (What is that called in Danish?). The past form is "hed", which is short and easy to overlook.

sentence.en: My name is Peter.

at hente.explanation: "At hente" means to fetch or to pick up, like collecting a person or a thing. "Jeg henter børnene i skole" means "I pick the children up from school". "Kan du hente en kop kaffe?" means "Can you get a cup of coffee?".

sentence.en: I pick up the children at three o'clock.

at hjælpe.explanation: "At hjælpe" means to help. You help someone with "hjælpe nogen": "Kan jeg hjælpe dig?" (Can I help you?). "Hjælp!" is also what you shout in an emergency.

sentence.en: Can I help you with something?

at hjælpe med.explanation: "At hjælpe med" means to help with something. After "med" comes the task: "hjælpe med lektierne" (help with the homework). To say who you help, put the person first: "Jeg hjælper dig med maden".

sentence.en: I help you with the food.

at holde.explanation: "At holde" means to hold or to keep. "Hold min taske" means "Hold my bag". It is also used in many fixed phrases: "holde en fest" (to throw a party), "holde af" (to be fond of) and "holde pause" (to take a break). The past form "holdt" and the "have" form "holdt" look the same.

sentence.da: Kan du **holde** min taske et øjeblik?
sentence.en: Can you hold my bag for a moment?

at hoppe.explanation: "At hoppe" means to jump, for example into water, over a puddle or on a trampoline. It is a lively everyday word. You can add small words to show the direction: "hoppe op" (jump up), "hoppe ned" (jump down) and "hoppe i" (jump in).

sentence.en: The children jump into the water.

at hoste.explanation: "At hoste" means to cough. The cough itself is "en hoste". You will hear it when someone has a cold: "Jeg hoster meget" means "I cough a lot".

sentence.en: I cough all night.

at huske.explanation: "At huske" means to remember, both to recall something and to remember to do something. "Husk at ringe" is "Remember to call", and "Husk!" on its own is a quick reminder. The opposite is "at glemme" (to forget), and "at huske på" means to keep something in mind.

sentence.en: I can't remember his name.

at håbe.explanation: "At håbe" means to hope: "Jeg håber, det går godt" (I hope it goes well). It is a very common way to be polite, as in "Jeg håber, du har det godt" (I hope you are well). The word for hope itself is "et håb".

sentence.en: I hope you are well.

at høre.explanation: "At høre" means to hear: "Jeg hører en lyd" (I hear a sound). It is also used when you get news, as in "Jeg har hørt, at han flytter" (I have heard he is moving). On the phone, "Vi hører fra dig" is a way to say we will hear from you. For listening on purpose, use "at lytte".

sentence.en: I can't hear you.

en hals.explanation: "En hals" covers both the neck and the throat. Danish does not separate them, so the meaning comes from the situation. "Jeg har ondt i halsen" means "I have a sore throat", and a necklace is "en halskæde", which uses the same word.

sentence.en: I have a sore throat.

en halv time.explanation: "En halv time" means half an hour, 30 minutes. "Halv" means half, and "time" is hour. Careful with clock times: "halv fem" means half past four (half an hour toward five), not half past five. The set phrase "en halv time" is simple and safe.

sentence.en: The bus comes in half an hour.

en handske.explanation: "En handske" is one glove. Since gloves come in pairs, you mostly hear the plural "handsker". The word starts with "hånd" (hand), so it is the thing you put on your hand. If you lose one, say "Jeg har mistet en handske" (I have lost a glove).

sentence.en: I have lost a glove.

en hat.explanation: "En hat" is a hat, usually one with a brim, like a sun hat or a fine hat for a party. It is not the same as "en hue" (a warm knitted cap) or "en kasket" (a cap with a peak). The plural just adds an "e", and you can say "hatten" for the hat. Note the double t: "hatten" and "hatte".

sentence.en: She is wearing a big hat.

en have.explanation: "En have" means a garden, the green area by a house. In Danish, 'the garden' is "haven" and the plural is "haver". Be careful: "at have" is the verb 'to have', which looks the same. "I haven" means 'in the garden'.

sentence.en: We are sitting in the garden.

en hest.explanation: "En hest" is a horse. The plural "heste" adds -e. To ride is "at ride", so "at ride på hest" is horseback riding. A small horse or pony is "en pony", and a farm with horses is a common sight in the Danish countryside.

sentence.en: The horse runs fast.

en himmel.explanation: En himmel is a sky, and it can also mean heaven. In daily talk you nearly always use "himlen" (the sky), which loses the "me" in the middle, so it is not "himmelen". You say "på himlen" for "in the sky". If you want to say it is cloudy, say "Himlen er grå" or "Det er skyet".

sentence.en: The sky is blue today.

en historie.explanation: "En historie" has two meanings: a story that someone tells, and history, the past (also the school lesson). Context makes it clear which one is meant. "Fortæl en historie" is "tell a story", while "Danmarks historie" is the history of Denmark. The plural is "historier".

sentence.en: He tells a funny story.

en hjemmesko.explanation: "En hjemmesko" is a slipper, a soft shoe you wear at home. It is built from "hjemme" (at home) and "sko" (shoe), so it means a shoe for home. Since many Danes take off their outdoor shoes in the hall, you will often see "hjemmesko" by the door. The plural is the same as the single word.

sentence.en: Put your slippers on.

en hobby.explanation: "En hobby" is something you like to do in your free time, just as in English. A common question is "Hvad er din hobby?" (What is your hobby?). Danes often say "Jeg har mange hobbyer" when they have several interests.

sentence.en: My hobby is painting.

en hoste.explanation: "En hoste" is a cough. The same word is also the action: "at hoste" means to cough. People say "Jeg har en hoste" or "Jeg har hoste". It is often paired with "forkølelse" (a cold).

sentence.en: I have a bad cough.

en hovedbanegård.explanation: "Hovedbanegård" is the main train station of a city, and in Copenhagen it is simply "Hovedbanegården". It is built from "hoved" (main), "bane" (railway) and "gård" (yard). The word is long, so say it in parts: HO-ved-ba-ne-gård. Note that "gård" becomes "gården" when you add "the".

sentence.en: We meet at the central station.

en hovedpine.explanation: "En hovedpine" is a headache, made from "hoved" (head) and "pine" (pain or torment). You say "Jeg har hovedpine" without "en" when you mean you currently have one. You can use "ondt i hovedet" with the same meaning.

sentence.da: Jeg har **hovedpine**, så jeg tager en pille.
sentence.en: I have a headache, so I am taking a pill.

en hovedret.explanation: "En hovedret" is the main course of a meal. It is built from "hoved" (head, main) and "ret" (dish), so it is the main dish. On menus the three parts are usually "forret", "hovedret" and "dessert".

sentence.en: For the main course I will have fish.

en hue.explanation: "En hue" is a knitted or woollen cap that keeps your head warm, like a beanie. Danes wear it all through the cold, dark winter. It is different from "en hat", which has a brim, and "en kasket", which is a cap with a peak. A small tip: children's winter hats are always "huer".

sentence.en: I am wearing a warm beanie.

en hund.explanation: "En hund" is a dog. Danes are very fond of dogs, and you will often hear "Må jeg klappe din hund?" (May I pet your dog?). A puppy is "en hvalp", and "at gø" is the verb for barking.

sentence.en: My dog is called Max.

en hvidvin.explanation: "En hvidvin" is a white wine. It is made of "hvid" (white) and "vin" (wine) and written as one word. White wine is a common choice with fish, and you can order it by the glass: "et glas hvidvin".

sentence.da: Vi bestiller en flaske **hvidvin** til fisken.
sentence.en: We order a bottle of white wine for the fish.

en hånd.explanation: "En hånd" is a hand. The word for more than one changes its vowel: "hænder". A very common phrase is "Vask dine hænder" (Wash your hands). Shaking hands is "at give hånd" or "at give hinanden hånden".

sentence.en: Wash your hands before we eat.

en hæl.explanation: "En hæl" is the back part of your foot, and also the raised back part of a shoe. And the word for more than one is "hæle". If your heel hurts, say "Min hæl gør ondt". High-heeled shoes are called "sko med høje hæle".

sentence.en: My heel hurts.

en hæveautomat.explanation: "En hæveautomat" is an ATM, a machine where you take out cash. It comes from "at hæve" (to withdraw money) and "automat" (machine). You say "at hæve penge" for to withdraw money. Cash is less common in Denmark, and many shops prefer cards.

sentence.en: Is there an ATM nearby?

et hav.explanation: Et hav is a sea or an ocean, a big body of salty water. In Danish, "the sea" is "havet", and you say "ved havet" for "by the sea". For a lake with fresh water use "en sø" instead. Denmark is surrounded by sea, so this word comes up a lot in everyday talk about holidays and weather.

sentence.en: The children are playing by the sea.

et hjem.explanation: "Et hjem" means a home, the place where you live and feel at home. It is not just the building (that is "et hus"). The word "hjemme" means 'at home' and "hjem" alone means 'toward home', as in "jeg går hjem". The plural is the same, "hjem".

sentence.en: I miss my home.

et hjerte.explanation: "Et hjerte" is a heart. The first letters "hj" sound like a simple "y". It is used both for the organ and for feelings, for example "med hele mit hjerte" (with all my heart). Hearts are also a card suit in card games.

sentence.en: My heart is beating fast.

et hospital.explanation: "Et hospital" is a hospital. For an emergency you go to "skadestuen" (the emergency room), and the emergency number in Denmark is 112. Danes often say "på hospitalet" for being at the hospital.

sentence.en: My mother is in the hospital.

et hotel.explanation: Et hotel is a hotel. And the spelling changes a bit: "the hotel" is "hotellet" with a double l, and more than one is "hoteller". You say "på hotellet" for "at the hotel". For a cheaper place to sleep you can look for "et vandrerhjem" (a hostel).

sentence.da: Vi bor på **hotellet** i to nætter.
sentence.en: We stay at the hotel for two nights.

et hotelværelse.explanation: "Et hotelværelse" is a room in a hotel, built from "hotel" and "værelse" (room). You can describe it with words such as "enkeltværelse" (single) or "dobbeltværelse" (double). The word "værelse" alone can also mean any room you rent or sleep in.

sentence.en: My hotel room has a view of the harbour.

et hoved.explanation: "Et hoved" is the head. And in Danish you use "the" form where English uses "my": "Jeg har ondt i hovedet" means "My head hurts". It also appears in compounds like "hovedpine" (headache) and "hovedstad" (capital city).

sentence.en: My head hurts.

et hus.explanation: "Et hus" means a house, a building where people live. It is "huset" for 'the house' and the plural is "huse". Don't mix it up with "et hjem" (a home), which is about the feeling of where you live rather than the building.

sentence.en: We live in a big house.

hallo.explanation: "Hallo" is used when you answer the phone and when you call out to get someone's attention. It is not the main word for a face-to-face greeting, where Danes prefer "hej". Said sharply, "hallo!" can also mean "hey, listen!".

sentence.en: Hello, can you hear me?

halv.explanation: "Halv" means half, and Danish telling of time works in a tricky way here: "halv fire" means half past three, not half past four. It counts to the next hour, so think "half way to four". Also "en halv" is half, as in "en halv liter" (half a liter).

sentence.en: We meet at half past seven.

forms.en: See you at half past six.

halv tre.explanation: Here is a big pitfall: "halv tre" means half past TWO, not half past three. Danes count half an hour toward the next hour, so "halv tre" is half way to three. So 2:30 is "halv tre", and 6:30 is "halv syv". Remember it as "half to three".

sentence.en: We eat lunch at half past eleven.

halvdelen.explanation: "Halvdelen" means the half, with "the" added on the end of an en-word. You usually say what it is half of with "af": "halvdelen af kagen" (half of the cake). If you simply mean half a thing, use "halv" or "en halv", as in "en halv liter".

sentence.en: I have eaten half of the cake.

halvfems.explanation: "Halvfems" means ninety. It is short for "halvfemsindstyve", an old counting system based on twenties: it literally means "half-way to five times twenty" (4.5 x 20 = 90). That is why Danish numbers feel odd at first. It is written as one word: you say "halvfems" for 90 and "enoghalvfems" for 91.

sentence.en: My grandfather is ninety years old.

halvfjerds.explanation: Means "seventy". It looks odd because Danish counts 70 as "half of four twenties", meaning 3.5 times twenty. It is shortened from an older, longer word. Note the "fj" at the start of the second part.

sentence.en: My grandmother is seventy years old.

halvtreds.explanation: Means "fifty". It looks odd because Danish counts 50 as "half of three twenties", meaning 2.5 times twenty. It is shortened from an older, longer word. The next numbers, tres, halvfjerds and firs, follow the same system.

sentence.en: The book costs fifty kroner.

ham.explanation: "Ham" means "him". It is used when something is done to a man or a boy, and also after words like "til" and "med". When he is the one doing it, you say "han". Be careful to keep it apart from "hans" (his).

sentence.en: I know him well.

han.explanation: "Han" means he, and it is used for a man or a boy. Its other form is "ham" (him), used after the action: "Jeg ser ham" (I see him). The word for "his" is "hans", and it never changes. The word for "she" is "hun", and for things Danes use "den" or "det".

sentence.en: He works in a bank.

handsker.explanation: "Handsker" means gloves, the plural of "en handske". Gloves come in pairs, so you usually talk about them in the plural, and "et par handsker" means a pair of gloves. The word starts with "hand" (hand). You put gloves on your hands, and mittens are "vanter".

sentence.en: I have forgotten my gloves at home.

hans.explanation: "Hans" means "his". It never changes, whether the thing is an en-word, an et-word or many things: "hans bil", "hans hus", "hans venner". It is only for a man or a boy. Do not mix it up with "ham" (him) or "han" (he).

sentence.en: That is his car.

hav en god dag.explanation: "Hav en god dag" means "have a good day" and is a friendly goodbye in shops and offices. "Hav" is a command form of "at have". Swap "dag" for "aften" (evening) or "weekend". The reply is "i lige måde".

sentence.da: Tak for hjælpen. **Hav en god dag!**
sentence.en: Thanks for the help. Have a good day!

hej.explanation: "Hej" means "hi" or "hello" and is used with almost everyone, friends and strangers, young and old. It is also used when you leave, often as "hej hej" (bye bye), which can be confusing at first. In shops people say "hej" both when you come in and when you go out. It is pronounced like the English "hi".

sentence.en: Hi, my name is Anna.

hej med dig.explanation: A warm, informal greeting that Danes use both when they meet and when they part, so the meaning depends on the moment. It is friendly and relaxed, good with friends, neighbours and shop staff. For several people, say "hej med jer". Tip: "hej hej" (said twice) is mostly used for saying goodbye.

sentence.en: Hi there, how is it going?

hejsa.explanation: "Hejsa" is a cheerful, informal version of "hej", like "hi there" or "hey". Use it with friends, family and children. It is not for formal situations, where "goddag" is better. You can also say "hej hej", but that is more often used for goodbye.

sentence.en: Hi there, what are you doing?

helbred.explanation: "Helbred" is health, meaning how well your body is doing. It is an et-word. "Godt helbred" is good health and "dårligt helbred" is poor health. "Helbred" is a little more formal than "sundhed", which is also used in general talk.

sentence.en: He has good health.

held og lykke.explanation: "Held og lykke" literally means "luck and happiness" and is the normal way to wish someone good luck before an exam, interview or new start. You can add "med" and what it is about: "held og lykke med prøven". A shorter, more casual version is just "held!" among friends.

sentence.da: **Held og lykke** med dit nye job!
sentence.en: Good luck with your new job!

heldig.explanation: "Heldig" means lucky. It comes from "held" (luck), and it gets a "t" with et-words ("et heldigt valg"). A common phrase is "Du er heldig" (You are lucky). The opposite is "uheldig" (unlucky), made by adding "u" at the front.

sentence.en: You are really lucky.

hele tiden.explanation: "Hele tiden" means all the time, or constantly. The word "tiden" is "the time" and "hele" is the whole. It can be a little negative, as in a thing that keeps happening and is annoying. For a milder "often", use "tit" or "ofte".

sentence.en: My phone rings all the time.

heller.explanation: "Heller" is used in sentences with "ikke" or "aldrig" to mean "either" or "neither", as in "heller ikke". In a positive sentence you use "også" (also) instead. A handy tip: "også" for yes-sentences, "heller ikke" for no-sentences.

sentence.da: Jeg kan **heller** ikke komme i dag.
sentence.en: I can't come today either.

forms.da: hellere i dag end i morgen

hellere.explanation: "Hellere" means rather, and it is used to say what you would prefer or what is the better choice: "Jeg vil hellere have te". It is the middle step between "gerne" (gladly) and "helst" (most of all). Do not mix it up with "heller" in "heller ikke".

sentence.da: Jeg vil **hellere** have te end kaffe.
sentence.en: I would rather have tea than coffee.

helst.explanation: "Helst" means preferably or most of all, and it shows your first choice. Think of the three steps: "gerne" (gladly), "hellere" (rather), "helst" (most of all). "Helst ikke" is a soft way to say "I would rather not".

sentence.en: I would most like to stay at home.

helt.explanation: "Helt" means "completely", "totally" or "entirely". It makes the next word stronger, as in "helt rigtigt" (completely right) or "helt sikker" (totally sure). It is very common in everyday talk. It is related to "hel" (whole), which is a different word used for things being in one piece. Use "helt" when you want to say all the way.

sentence.en: I completely agree with you.

hende.explanation: "Hende" means "her" when something is done to a woman or a girl, or after words like "til" and "med". When she is the one doing it, you say "hun". Do not mix it up with "hendes", which means "her" in the sense of belonging to her, like "hendes bil".

sentence.en: I like her.

hendes.explanation: "Hendes" means "her" or "hers". It never changes, whether the thing is an en-word, an et-word or many things. It is only for a woman or a girl. Do not mix it up with "hende" (her, after a verb) or "hun" (she).

sentence.en: That is her bag.

her.explanation: "Her" means "here", the place where you are. "Kom her" means "Come here". It also helps make "this" in everyday speech: "den her bog" (this book). Do not mix it up with "der" (there), and do not confuse it with "hende" (her).

sentence.en: I live here in the town.

herinde.explanation: "Herinde" means in here, and it is used when you are inside and talking about the place around you. The partner word for further away is "derinde". When someone moves in, Danish uses "ind", as in "Kom ind!".

sentence.en: It is warm in here.

hinanden.explanation: "Hinanden" means each other or one another, and it is used when two or more people do the same thing to one another. It never changes form. It usually comes after the action word, often with a small word like "på" or "med" in front: "snakke med hinanden".

sentence.en: They help each other.

hjem.explanation: "Hjem" means home when you are going or moving towards it, so it goes with verbs like "gå" (go), "køre" (drive) and "komme" (come). When you are already there it is "hjemme". Note that Danish needs no "to": "gå hjem" is simply to go home.

sentence.en: I am going home now.

hjemme.explanation: "Hjemme" means at home, and it tells you where someone is, not where they go. Use it with "er" (am, is, are) and "bliver" (stay): "Jeg bliver hjemme" (I'm staying home). When you are going there, use "hjem" instead.

sentence.en: I am at home tonight.

hjælp.explanation: "Hjælp" means help, and it is an en-word, so "the help" is "hjælpen". It is used without "en" in front, as in "Jeg har brug for hjælp" (I need help). It is also what you shout in an emergency: "Hjælp!". The verb is "at hjælpe". A polite way to thank someone is "Tak for hjælpen".

sentence.en: I need help.

holland.explanation: "Holland" is the Netherlands. Place names like this are written with a capital letter and used without "the": "i Holland" means "in the Netherlands" and "til Holland" means "to the Netherlands". Danes say "Holland" for the whole country, although the official name is "Nederlandene". A person is "en hollænder" and the language is "hollandsk".

sentence.en: Many people cycle in the Netherlands.

hollandsk.explanation: "Hollandsk" means Dutch, both for things from the Netherlands and for the language. It is written with a small letter, and it stays the same before an et-word because it already ends in -sk. Danes say "Holland" for the country in everyday speech, and "Nederlandene" is the more formal name.

sentence.en: He speaks Dutch with his family.

honning.explanation: "Honning" is honey, an en-word, so "the honey" is "honningen". It is usually used without "en", like "lidt honning" (a little honey). It is common in tea, on bread and in yoghurt, and "honningkage" is a spiced Danish Christmas cake.

sentence.da: Jeg tager lidt **honning** i min te.
sentence.en: I take a little honey in my tea.

hos.explanation: "Hos" means at someone's place, and it is always followed by a person: "hos mig", "hos lægen", "hos frisøren". For places and buildings you use another word such as "på" or "i". It is very useful: "Jeg er hos min ven".

sentence.da: Jeg sover **hos** min ven i nat.
sentence.en: I am sleeping at my friend's place tonight.

hud.explanation: "Hud" is the skin, on your body, and it is an en-word. People mostly say "huden" (the skin) in sentences like "Min hud er tør" (My skin is dry). You will see it in pharmacy talk with "hudcreme" (skin cream).

sentence.en: My skin is very dry.

hun.explanation: "Hun" means she, and you use it for a woman or a girl. It is what you say when you are the one doing something. When it comes after a verb, like "Ser hun?", it still stays "hun". For the other direction, "hende" is used instead, as in "Jeg ser hende".

related.en: her / she (after a verb or word like 'to')

sentence.en: She lives in Copenhagen.

hundrede.explanation: "Hundrede" means one hundred. It stays the same after other numbers, so you say "to hundrede" (200) and "tre hundrede" (300). You can say "hundrede" alone for 100, and Danes often say "et hundrede" only when they want to stress the exact number. Prices in kroner are a very common place to meet this word.

sentence.en: The book costs a hundred kroner.

hurtig.explanation: "Hurtig" means fast or quick, for people, cars, answers and actions. When you want to say that something happens quickly, use the form with "t" at the end: "Han løber hurtigt" (He runs fast). The opposite is "langsom" (slow). "Skynd dig" is the everyday way to tell someone to hurry up.

sentence.en: The train is very fast.

hvad.explanation: "Hvad" means "what" and is one of the most useful question words. "Hvad er det?" means "What is that?" and "Hvad laver du?" means "What are you doing?". Said by itself, "Hvad?" can mean "Pardon?", but it can sound a bit blunt, so "Undskyld?" is more polite. It is also used for "what" in sentences like "Jeg ved, hvad du mener" (I know what you mean).

sentence.en: What is your name?

hvad betyder det?.explanation: "Hvad betyder det?" means "What does that mean?" and is great for learning new words. "At betyde" is the verb for "to mean". You can ask about a particular word with "Hvad betyder..?", for example "Hvad betyder 'dejlig'?". You can also use it about a sign or a sentence you saw. Danes will often explain in simple Danish or English.

sentence.en: What does that word mean?

hvad er klokken?.explanation: The standard way to ask what time it is. "Klokken" literally means "the clock", so the question is "what is the clock?". You answer with "klokken er" plus the time. Another polite way is "ved du, hvad klokken er?" (do you know what time it is?).

sentence.en: Excuse me, what time is it?

forms.en: What is that called in Danish?
What is that called in English?

hvad hedder det på dansk?.explanation: "Hvad hedder det på dansk?" is a great question for learners: "what is that called in Danish?". The verb "hedder" means "is called", the same word used for names ("jeg hedder Anna"). Swap "dansk" for another language to ask about it. Point at something while you ask.

sentence.da: Hvad er det? **Hvad hedder det på dansk?**
sentence.en: What is that? What is that called in Danish?

hvad hedder du?.explanation: "Hvad hedder du?" means "What's your name?" and literally "What are you called?". It uses the verb "at hedde" (to be called), not "at have" or "at være". You answer with "Jeg hedder.." (My name is..). For another person, use "hvad hedder han?" or "hvad hedder hun?". It is polite and used with all ages.

sentence.en: What's your name? - My name is Anna.

hvad koster det?.explanation: "Hvad koster det?" means "how much does it cost?". Use "det" for et-words and "den" for en-words, so "hvad koster den?" for an en-word like "en bog". For several things say "hvad koster de?". Good for shops and markets.

sentence.da: **Hvad koster det?** Jeg vil gerne købe den.
sentence.en: How much does it cost? I'd like to buy it.

forms.en: What are you doing at the weekend?

hvad laver du?.explanation: "Hvad laver du?" means "what are you doing?" and can mean right now or in general, like "what do you do?". The word "laver" comes from "at lave", to make or do. For a job question, "hvad arbejder du med?" is clearer. Use "hvad laver I?" with several people.

sentence.en: What are you doing tonight?

hvad med dig?.explanation: Use this to turn a question back to the other person, like "How about you?" in English. It is a very handy way to keep a conversation going after answering. Use "hvad med jer?" for more than one person. You can put anyone in place of "dig", for example "hvad med Anna?".

sentence.da: Jeg har det godt. **Hvad med dig?**
sentence.en: I'm doing well. What about you?

hvad så?.explanation: "Hvad så?" literally means "what then?" and is a casual greeting like "what's up?" or "how's it going?". Friends use it in place of "hvordan har du det?". You can reply "det går fint", "ikke så meget" or just "hvad så med dig?". Keep it for friends and people your own age.

sentence.en: Hi Anna, what's up?

hvem.explanation: "Hvem" means "who" and is used when you ask about a person, as in "Hvem er det?" (Who is that?). It is the same word whether you ask about one person or many. It also works after a word like "til" or "med", as in "Med hvem?" (With whom?). The word "hvis" means "whose", but it is also a different word meaning "if", so be careful.

sentence.en: Who is your teacher?

hver.explanation: "Hver" means "each" or "every" and is used with one thing, like "hver dag" (every day) or "hver morgen" (every morning). It is used with en-words; for et-words you say "hvert", as in "hvert år" (every year). For "all" of them together, use "alle".

sentence.en: I run every morning.

hver dag.explanation: "Hver dag" means every day. "Hver" means each or every and is used with an en-word like "dag". With an et-word, it is "hvert", as in "hvert år" (every year). Another way to say the same thing is "alle dage", but "hver dag" is far more common.

sentence.en: I drink coffee every day.

hvert.explanation: "Hvert" means each or every, and it is used with et-words: "hvert år", "hvert hus". With en-words you use "hver" instead: "hver dag", "hver bil". Both are followed by a single thing, not a plural.

sentence.en: We travel to Sweden every year.

hvid.explanation: "Hvid" means white. Like most colour words, it gets a "t" with et-words ("et hvidt hus") and an "e" when there is more than one ("hvide biler"). The opposite is "sort" (black). Watch the "hv" at the start: the h is silent, so it sounds like "vi(th)".

sentence.en: I have a white cat.

hvidløg.explanation: "Hvidløg" is garlic. It is built from "hvid" (white) and "løg" (onion), so it is literally a white onion. It is an et-word, so "the garlic" is "hvidløget". One clove is "et fed hvidløg". It is used for flavour in many dishes.

sentence.en: I put garlic in the sauce.

hvilken.explanation: "Hvilken" means "which" and asks you to choose between things. It changes its ending to match the word that follows it: "hvilken" for en-words (hvilken bil), "hvilket" for et-words (hvilket hus), and "hvilke" for more than one (hvilke bøger). It is also used for "what kind" in questions like "Hvilken farve?" (Which colour?). Use "hvad" when you don't mean a choice.

sentence.en: Which colour do you like best?

hvis.explanation: "Hvis" means if, and it sets a condition: "Hvis det regner, bliver vi hjemme". Do not mix it up with "om", which means "whether": "Jeg ved ikke, om han kommer". "Hvis" can also mean "whose", but "if" is far more common.

sentence.en: If it rains, we stay at home.

hvor.explanation: "Hvor" means "where" and starts questions about a place, as in "Hvor bor du?" (Where do you live?). It also joins with other words: "hvor meget" (how much), "hvor mange" (how many), "hvor gammel" (how old). When you ask about direction, use "hvorhen" (where to) or "hvor.. hen". Danish uses "hvor" in many question starters.

sentence.en: Where do you live?

hvor er toilettet?.explanation: "Hvor er toilettet?" means "where is the restroom?". The word "toilet" is an et-word, and "the" is added on the end to give "toilettet". You may see "WC" on signs. Add "henne" for a natural, friendly feel. Say "undskyld" first to be polite.

sentence.en: Excuse me, where is the restroom?

hvor gammel er du?.explanation: "Hvor gammel er du?" means "How old are you?" and it is built from "hvor" (how) and "gammel" (old). You answer with "Jeg er.. år (gammel)" (I am.. years old). The word "år" means "year", and in Danish you often leave out "gammel" in the answer. Danish uses "er" (am/are) here, not "have" as some languages do. It is fine with friends, but think about whether it fits with adults you don't know.

sentence.da: **Hvor gammel er du?** - Jeg er tyve år.
sentence.en: How old are you? - I am twenty years old.

forms.en: Where do you all come from?

hvor kommer du fra?.explanation: "Hvor kommer du fra?" means "Where are you from?" and literally "Where do you come from?". You answer with "Jeg kommer fra.." and then the country or town. Note that "fra" stays at the end of the question, which is different from the way some English speakers might say it. It is a common way to start a conversation with someone new.

sentence.da: **Hvor kommer du fra?** - Jeg kommer fra England.
sentence.en: Where are you from? - I'm from England.

forms.en: How much does it cost? (an en-word)

hvor meget koster det?.explanation: "Hvor meget koster det?" means "How much does it cost?" and is a must for shopping. "At koste" is the verb for "to cost". "Det" means "it". For an en-word you can say "den" instead, as in "Hvor meget koster den?", and for more than one thing, "de". The price is given in "kroner" (crowns), so you may hear "tyve kroner" (twenty kroner).

sentence.en: Excuse me, how much does it cost?

hvordan.explanation: "Hvordan" means "how" and asks about the way something is done or what something is like. "Hvordan har du det?" is a common way to ask how someone is doing. "Hvordan går det?" means "How is it going?". Don't use "hvordan" for "how much" or "how many"; use "hvor meget" and "hvor mange" for those.

sentence.en: How do I get to the station?

hvordan går det?.explanation: "Hvordan går det?" means "How's it going?" and is a very common way to ask how someone is doing. It is friendlier and more casual than a long formal greeting. A normal answer is "Det går godt, tak" (It's going well, thanks), and you can add "og dig?" (and you?) to ask back. Another very common choice is "Hvordan har du det?".

sentence.da: **Hvordan går det?** - Det går godt, tak.
sentence.en: How's it going? - It's going well, thanks.

hvordan har du det?.explanation: The usual way to ask someone how they are. Literally it means "how have you it?". Answer with "jeg har det godt" or "fint, tak". With more than one person, say "hvordan har I det?". In a quick chat, Danes also say "hvordan går det?" (how is it going?).

sentence.en: Hi Peter! How are you?

hvorfor.explanation: "Hvorfor" means "why" and asks for a reason. The answer often starts with "fordi" (because). Note the order: after "hvorfor", the verb comes next, as in "Hvorfor kommer du?" (Why are you coming?). It is built from "hvor" and "for", which is why it has two parts. Short and handy: "Hvorfor ikke?" (Why not?).

sentence.en: Why are you so happy?

hvornår.explanation: "Hvornår" means "when" in a question, as in "Hvornår kommer toget?" (When does the train come?). It only asks about time. For "when" in the middle of a sentence, as in "I was happy when you came", Danish uses "da" or "når" instead. A tip: the "når" part inside "hvornår" is a small clue that both words are about time.

related.en: when (in a sentence, repeated or in the future)

sentence.en: When does the shop open?

hyggelig.explanation: "Hyggelig" means cozy, pleasant or nice, and it comes from the Danish idea of "hygge". It describes a place, an evening or a person: "Han er hyggelig" is "He is nice to be around". With et-words it gets a "t" ("et hyggeligt sted"). There is no perfect English word for it.

sentence.en: It was a cozy evening.

hyggeligt at møde dig.explanation: "Hyggeligt at møde dig" is the phrase for "nice to meet you". The word "hyggelig" is a warm, cozy word that Danes love, and it fits many situations. Reply "i lige måde" or "i lige måde, hyggeligt". For a friend you already know, use "hyggeligt at se dig" instead.

sentence.da: Jeg hedder Maja. **Hyggeligt at møde dig.**
sentence.en: I'm Maja. Nice to meet you.

håndbagage.explanation: "Håndbagage" is the small luggage you take with you on to a plane, built from "hånd" (hand) and "bagage" (luggage). It is an en-word with no plural, like "bagage". Airlines say "Du må have en stk. håndbagage" about the size and number you may bring.

sentence.en: I am only travelling with carry-on luggage.

håndbold.explanation: "Håndbold" is handball, a team sport that is very popular in Denmark. The word is used without "en" when you talk about the sport: "Jeg spiller håndbold". It is built from "hånd" (hand) and "bold" (ball).

sentence.da: Hun spiller **håndbold** to gange om ugen.
sentence.en: She plays handball twice a week.

hår.explanation: "Hår" is hair, and it is an et-word. Unlike English, "hår" on your head is normally just "håret" (the hair): "Hun har langt hår" (She has long hair). One single strand is "et hår", and "at have langt hår" is the usual way to describe it.

sentence.en: She has long hair.

hård.explanation: "Hård" means hard, either physically (hard like a rock) or hard to deal with ("et hårdt job"). With et-words it gets a "t" ("et hårdt job") and with more than one an "e" ("hårde sten"). Be careful: for "hard" meaning "difficult", Danes usually say "svær".

sentence.en: The bed is too hard.

høj.explanation: "Høj" means tall or high, both for people and for things. With an et-word it takes "-t" (højt), and with many things "-e" (høje). "Højt" is also how you say "loudly": "Tal højt" means "Speak loudly". The opposite is "lav" (low or short), and "højere" means taller or higher.

sentence.en: He is very tall.

højre.explanation: "Højre" means right, as in the right side or the right hand. It stays the same whatever word it describes. It is the opposite of "venstre" (left). For directions you usually say "til højre" (to the right), and "højre" can also be a word for the right side of the road.

sentence.en: I write with my right hand.
